senses.gloss:
kanyā
(‘unmarried girl’)
------------------------------------------
An unmarried girl (a maiden)—about ten years in age has been called a ‘kanyā’ in the Hindu scriptures.
A कन्या was supposed to be under the protection of सोम, Gandharva and अग्नि before her मर्रिअगे.
Though the मर्रिअगे of a girl was primarily the responsibility of her ड़थेर् (or brother, in case the ड़थेर् is not alive), she was free to select her husband in case they failed in their duty.
The qualifications prescribed for a कन्या or a bride, have changed over the centuries. A few of the most common and general qualifications are: bāndhavam or purity of the family; rūpam (beauty); prajñā (intelligence); and, vittam (wealth) (vide Bhāradvāja Gṛhyasūtras 1.6).
Kanyās without brothers, with awkward names and whose virginity was in doubt were to be avoided.
Sale of girls in मर्रिअगे, which seems to have existed in ancient times—as was the case in many other countries—was severely condemned by the धर्मसूत्रस् and निबन्धस् (digests). Whatever money or property was taken by the girl’s ड़थेर् (as kanyāśulka) from the bridegroom’s family, was to be given back to the newly married couple for their maintenance.
Though during the period 600 B. C. to A. D. 200, the age of a girl for मर्रिअगे was not seriously considered or limits fixed, popular feeling seems to have swung towards early (pre-puberty) marriages 1. Reasons cited by some competent authorities for this trend are: spread of बुद्धिस्म् and a cheap kind of मोनस्तिचिस्म्; laxity of morals among the nuns; lack of एदुचतिओन् among girls; मर्रिअगे for girls being looked upon as an equivalent of the उपनयन for boys and hence the fixing of the age for मर्रिअगे as eight years. For a girl to remain unmarried and die as a spinster was generally disliked.
Kanyā (Virgo) is one of the twelve ज़ोदिअचल् सिग्न्स् or constellations (the sixth) in अस्त्रोलोग्य्. The Hastā and the Cittā are the main स्तर्स् in this.
Those born under this sign are supposed to be handsome in appearance, learned in many sciences, become wealthy but are religious by nature.

Kanyakā-Parameśvarī
------------------------------------------
She is the patron goddess of the वैश्य community, especially in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
It is said that once ब्रह्मा asked Jayanta, the son of इन्द्र, to fight and kill a demon Śatajihva by name. Śacīdevī, his मोथेर्, intervened and prevented him from going, out of fear that he himself may be killed in the process. This enraged ब्रह्मा who cursed her to be born on earth among the vaiśyas.
So, she was born as the daughter of Kusumaśreṣṭhi and was named वासवाम्बा. A king, Viṣṇuvardhana by name, proposed that she be given to him in मर्रिअगे. Since the members of the community refused permission, the king threatened to fight and kill them. But before he could do it, a large section of the community led by वासवाम्बा herself, immolated themselves in fire. She was in course of time deified into the goddess Kanyakāparameśvarī. Her temples are found generally in places where the vaiśyas are concentrated.
Another story identifies her with पार्वती.

Kanyākumārī
------------------------------------------
Also known as ‘Kanyātīrtha,’ कन्या-kumārī is a very ancient place of पिल्ग्रिमगे of over two thousand years dedicated to the Divine मोथेर् in her aspect of a virgin. It is situated at the southernmost tip of India, in the कन्याकुमारी district of Tamil Nadu. It is very near Thiruva-nanthapuram (Trivandrum), the capital city of Kerala State, the distance being just 87 kms. (54 miles). It is on the sea-shore where the Indian ocean, the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian sea merge.
Kanyākumārī idol in the templeThere are two mythological accounts connected with this deity. The first tells us that the female child that escaped from the clutches of कṁस, assumed the form of दुर्गा and warned him about his killer कृष्ण living elsewhere, settled down here.
As per the second account, Puṇyakeśī, the daughter of Mayāsura (the chief architect of the असुरस् or demon race) performed severe तपस् or austerities here to get Lord शिव as her husband. शिव promised to marry her at the end of the कल्प or aeon but advised her to continue her तपस्. While she was doing so, a terrible demon Bāṇāsura pressed her to marry him. She was obliged to kill him by using her चक्र or discus. After this she resumed her तपस् and is still waiting for her final union with शिव.
According to another version the देवी was born as the daughter of a king in order to kill the demon Bāṇāsura who had become invincible by divine boons. Only a maiden could kill him.
When the देवी started meditating on Lord शिव and appealed to him to marry her, he came down from कैलास and was waiting at the town शुचीन्द्रम् for the auspicious moment, in order to come to her for the मर्रिअगे. The gods, afraid that their purpose of the Devi (as a maiden) killing Bāṇāsura would be rendered fruitless, made a fake cock crow so that शिव was roused from meditation. In utter dismay he found that the auspicious moment had passed off! So he remained at शुचीन्द्रम् itself. And, the देवी here was made to wait indefinitely with the garland in her hand, for शिव!
Of course, she did kill Bāṇāsura also who appeared there and fought with her.
The goddess is also known as Kātyā-yanī (daughter of the sage Katya), an aspect of पार्वती.
The image of the virgin goddess is in the standing posture with two arms. She is holding an अक्षमाला or rosary in her hand. There is a carved figure of siṁha or lion, suggesting that she is दुर्गा, on the pedestal.
There are four pillars in the temple which, when struck, emit musical sounds like those of a Mṛdaṅga (drum), Vīṇā (lute), flute and jalataraṅga (porcelain water cup instrument).
Apart from the देवी temple, there is also a beautiful and magnificent temple with an imposing image of Swami Vivekānanda, built on the bigger rock in the sea, not far from the coast. There is a regular ferry service from the coast to the temple.

kanyādāna
(‘gifting the maid [to the young man in मर्रिअगे]’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism considers मर्रिअगे as a sacrament. Husband and wife are fellow travellers and companions in the path of spiritual evolution.
When a suitable young man has been found as a match for his daughter, the ड़थेर् of the girl had to give her to him in a religious rite known as ‘kanyādāna’.
Kanyādāna is one of the several steps involved in the much bigger process called ‘vivāha’ or मर्रिअगे. The ड़थेर् of the bride tells the bride-groom in this rite that he should not prove false to the bride in धर्म, अर्थ and काम. The latter responds with the words, ‘nāticarāmi’ (‘I shall not do so.’).
This rite described in the ancient धर्मशास्त्रस् has practically remained the same even to this day.
See also ṢOḌAŚA-SAṀSKĀRAS and VIVĀHA.

Kanakadāsa
(A. D. 1508-1606)
------------------------------------------
Kanakadāsa, one of the four most important leaders of the Vaiṣṇava भक्ति Movement in Karnataka, is also an ideal example to show how भक्ति or devotion to God levels up human beings, transcending all barriers of caste or culture.
He was born at Kāginele, a small village near Dharwad in northern Karna-taka. He probably belonged to the dāsa, kuruba or beḍa community classed among the शूद्रस्. According to one version, he was the son of a chieftain of a small province, lost his all in a battle with the enemies, was critically injured but was miraculously saved by the grace of Ādikeśava (an aspect of Lord विष्णु) at whose command, became a haridāsa (servant of Lord Hari) or a saint. He was a disciple of Vyāsarāya (A. D. 1447-1539) a well-known Vaiṣṇava saṁnyāsin and the abbot of a monastery. पुरन्दरदास (A. D. 1484-1564) was his co-disciple.
He was a great devotee of God and a saint of a very high order. Quite a few miracles have been attributed to him. Some of them are: the image of कृष्ण in the temple at Udupi (Karnataka) turning around to the backside to give darśan to him, who was praying there since he had been denied entry into the main entrance; blasting of a big boulder that was proving an obstacle to a new tank under construction and so on.
Apart from a number of devotional songs in which he has used the words ‘Kāginele Ādikeśava’ as his pen-name, he has also composed the following poetical works: Mohanataraṅgiṇī (a poetical work of a mythological type); Naḷacaritre (story of Naḷa and दमयन्ती); Rāmadhānyacaritre (a humorous composition to prove the superiority of rāgi [a kind of millet] over rice); Haribhaktisāra (an ethico-devotional work) and Nṛsiṁhastava (a hymn on नरसिṁह, the man-lion इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु, now not available).
See also DĀSAKŪṬA and VYĀSARĀYA.
